units.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The resource organizes equivalences through prime-zero duality and distinguishes nearly tautological restatements from structurally surprising reformulations.
units.interpretation:
The survey presents RH equivalences as translations made possible by the explicit-formula duality between primes and zeros. Once that bridge is accepted, prime-counting error statements and zero-set statements become different surfaces of the same claim.

This span uses that idea at the overview level. It lists the Li(x)+O(x^(1/2+epsilon)) form, the von Koch bound, and Schoenfeld's explicit inequality as equivalent prime-side formulations, without trying to reprove them. The trainable content is the equivalence map itself: error structure is preserved while the visible objects change from zeros to prime counts.

units.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: Two attractive sufficient conditions are not merely unproved but known false, making the logical failure mode of an RH attack explicit.
units.interpretation:
This section is a failure map for auxiliary proof routes. Turan-type conditions say that certain zero-free regions for partial sums of zeta would imply RH, but Montgomery's theorem shows that those partial sums do in fact have zeros in the relevant half-plane. De Branges' positivity criterion would likewise force RH for a suitable Hilbert space H(E), but the natural choice E(z) = xi(1 - iz) fails the needed positivity condition.

The unit therefore records falsification of attractive representations, not support for a live criterion. Its mathematical content is the logical pattern "A implies RH, but A is false," with each failure attached to a specific auxiliary object rather than to vague pessimism.

units.title: A strengthening of the Nyman-Beurling criterion for the Riemann hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The Nyman-Beurling closure criterion is strengthened by replacing a continuous generating family with the much thinner natural-number subfamily.
units.interpretation:
The source starts from the Nyman-Beurling closure criterion in a Hilbert space of Beurling functions and then makes a sharper claim about what generators are actually needed. Instead of approximating chi with the full continuum of dilations, it proposes that the natural-number subfamily already carries the whole RH criterion.

That is a genuine thinning operation on the representation. The ambient closure problem stays the same, but the generating family is compressed from all real a >= 1 to integer a, turning the issue into whether the arithmetic skeleton B_nat is already enough.

units.title: A strengthening of the Nyman-Beurling criterion for the Riemann hypothesis
units.selection_reason: A natural finite approximation converges in weaker senses but diverges in the needed Hilbert norm; a parameterized, whole-range construction repairs the route under RH.
units.interpretation:
The unit identifies a precise failure mode in the Nyman-Beurling program: the natural finite approximants F_n and the Selberg approximation may converge in weaker senses, yet finite-scale combinations are obstructed in the Hilbert space H by a lower bound that makes any such convergence extremely slow.

The repair is to stop truncating the scale parameter. The paper defines f_s(x)=sum mu(a)rho_a(x)/a^s over the full range of a, interprets it as a correction of 1/zeta(s), and then claims that under RH one has f_epsilon in B_nat while unconditionally f_epsilon tends to -chi in H as epsilon decreases to 0. The move is analytic weighting in place of finite cutoff.

units.title: Problems of the Millennium: The Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The finite-field analogue becomes geometric through Frobenius and cohomology, providing strong but explicitly analogical evidence for the classical problem.
units.interpretation:
Bombieri presents the finite-field case as the strongest structural evidence for RH because the zeta function of a curve over F_q has an Euler product, functional equation, and a Zeta-function form whose zeros have absolute value q^(-1/2) in the RH case. He then broadens the picture to general varieties, where the characteristic roots, meaning the reciprocals of zeros and poles, are interpreted as Frobenius eigenvalues on etale cohomology.

The conceptual move is an analytic-to-geometric bridge. Classical zeta language is re-expressed through divisors, Frobenius, and cohomology, but the source is explicit that this remains evidence and analogy for the classical RH, not a mechanism that already proves the classical statement.

units.title: Problems of the Millennium: The Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: Weil's explicit formula is presented as a local-to-global prime/zero identity and, in the function-field case, as a Lefschetz trace formula.
units.interpretation:
The explicit formula is presented here as a single accounting identity joining transformed test-function values at 0, the nontrivial zeros, and 1 to a prime-power sum and local integral terms. The Mellin transform is the organizing device: once f is placed in Weil's class W, the same transformed test function can be read on both the zero side and the prime side.

The conceptual operation is a bridge from arithmetic data to trace language. The span then sharpens that bridge in the function-field case, where the same explicit formula is said to come from the Lefschetz fixed-point formula for Frobenius: the zero sum becomes the trace on cohomology, especially H^1, while the prime side becomes a fixed-point count. That makes the explicit formula a dictionary between zeros, primes, and traces rather than just a formal identity.

units.title: Trace formula in noncommutative geometry and the zeros of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: Zeros are reframed as missing spectral lines/resonances on an adele-class space, while the global trace formula—not merely the construction—is left equivalent to RH.
units.interpretation:
The paper proposes a spectral interpretation in which zeta zeros appear on the spectral side as an absorption spectrum: critical zeros appear directly, while noncritical zeros enter as resonances through their harmonic potential relative to the critical line. The span also reports preliminary spectral and trace-formula results on adele-class spaces, including local and finite-place trace formulas that recover the corresponding Weil explicit-formula terms, and it highlights the elimination of the auxiliary parameter delta.

The conceptual shift is from locating zeros to establishing a global trace formula whose spectral and geometric sides coincide. The source explicitly does not claim that global step is complete here: it says the global trace formula is left open and that its validity would be equivalent to RH for Groessencharakter L-functions. The excerpt is therefore an open spectral program with concrete local pieces, not a finished spectral proof.

units.title: Trace formula in noncommutative geometry and the zeros of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: Comparing semiclassical and Euler-product expansions predicts prime-labelled periodic orbits and broken time reversal, but exposes a sign and finite-repeat mismatch.
units.interpretation:
Connes compares a semiclassical periodic-orbit expansion for the oscillatory counting term with the Euler-product expansion coming from zeta. Read as an analogy, that term-by-term matching proposes what a hypothetical Riemann flow would have to look like: primitive orbits indexed by primes, period log p, instability exponent +/- log p, and no time-reversal symmetry.

The important content is not a finished flow but the obstructions the comparison exposes. The overall sign is wrong, and the finite-repeat denominator matches only asymptotically rather than exactly, so the span functions as a constraint-and-failure analysis for any spectral-dynamical model.

units.title: More than two fifths of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are on the critical line
units.selection_reason: The gain over Levinson is localized to a longer mollifier made possible by importing three distinct analytic, arithmetic, and error-control components.
units.interpretation:
The paper singles out one new ingredient relative to Levinson's theorem: the mollifier is extended from length T^(1/2) to T^(4/7). The source attributes that change to Deshouillers-Iwaniec bounds on averages of Kloosterman sums and then describes the paper as a synthesis of three earlier inputs.

The division of labor is concrete. One cited paper supplies the analytic reduction to a main term plus an error term with incomplete Kloosterman sums, another supplies the asymptotic formula for the main term, and Deshouillers-Iwaniec supplies the key lemma for the error term. In this span, the longer mollifier matters because the surrounding analytic, arithmetic, and error-control pieces are explicitly assembled to support it.

units.title: More than two fifths of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are on the critical line
units.selection_reason: The checked transcription identifies b(n,P), the endpoint conditions on P, delayed variational optimization, the zero-proportion objective, and the more general derivative combination.
units.context_limit: The v0 pdftotext span lost the coefficient, zero-counting, and general-combination formulas.

This repaired unit introduces freedom into Levinson's method at two levels. The mollifier coefficient b(n, P) is defined using a polynomial P with endpoint conditions P(0) = 0 and P(1) = 1, and P is said to be optimizable by calculus of variations. At the same time, the auxiliary object is widened from zeta(s) + a(s) zeta'(s) to a general derivative combination sum_n a_n(s) zeta^(n)(s).

The proof burden is therefore relocated from zeta itself to a tunable surrogate. The source explicitly ties that surrogate to the payoff: if the chosen combination has few enough zeros to the right of the critical line, one gets a lower bound on the proportion of zeta zeros on the critical line.

units.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The explicit formula is reframed as positivity, followed by Li's restricted sequence and the open need for an interpretation that makes positivity transparent.
units.interpretation:
Conrey presents Weil's explicit formula as a prime-zero duality and then turns RH into a positivity test. For admissible h of the stated quadratic form, nonnegativity of the zero sum becomes equivalent to RH.

Li's sequence makes that positivity problem discrete: the lambda_n are given both by a zero sum and by derivatives of log xi(s) at s = 1. The span's real content is this reframing from geometry of zeros to positivity of a functional or sequence, while also acknowledging that the source does not yet explain why those quantities should be positive.

units.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: A striking numerical spectral coincidence is diagnosed as a computational artifact, while the weaker trace/explicit-formula resemblance survives as a research direction.
units.interpretation:
The anecdote is a diagnostic about failed spectral evidence. Computed Laplacian eigenvalues seemed to contain ordinates of zeta zeros and zeros of L(s,chi_3), which would have had dramatic consequences because legitimate spectral occurrence would force the associated lambda values to be positive.

The source then explains that these were spurious eigenvalues tied to pseudo cusp forms and to the computation method. That failure is the point of the unit: an apparent Hilbert-Polya-type bridge collapses when the spectral data are not genuine, even though the broader resemblance between Selberg's trace formula and the explicit formula remains mathematically suggestive.

units.title: Random Matrix Theory and zeta(1/2+it)
units.selection_reason: Local zero statistics motivate transferring characteristic-polynomial calculations from CUE to zeta, with theorem, conjecture, numerics, and heuristic inputs kept distinct.
units.interpretation:
The span builds a local transfer principle from zeta zeros to random matrices. It reviews the conjecture that scaled zeta zeros on the mean-spacing scale have the same local statistics as CUE eigenphases, cites Montgomery's restricted-range theorem and numerical evidence, and then says that locally determined zeta statistics high on the critical line may be modeled by the corresponding statistics of CUE characteristic polynomials.

That is a concrete model-transfer bridge, but it is explicitly local and heuristic. The support is short-range spectral agreement, not a theorem about all value statistics of zeta, so the modeling claim has to stay attached to the scale restriction and the conjectural status of the transfer.

units.title: Random Matrix Theory and zeta(1/2+it)
units.selection_reason: Mean density fixes matrix size as a function of height; finite-height behavior is then split into a universal random-matrix component and an arithmetic prime contribution.
units.interpretation:
The span fixes the random-matrix/zeta bridge by matching mean densities, identifying the matrix size N with log(T/2pi) so that CUE eigenangles and zeta zeros have the same local average spacing. With that scale in place, the excerpt records proved CUE cumulant and value-distribution results, notes numerical agreement with zeta data under the same identification, and recalls that finite-T zeta correlations include both a random-matrix part and a prime-sum correction.

The conceptual payoff is a split between a universal local model and arithmetic finite-height corrections once the scale is fixed. But the span does not place all claims at the same epistemic level: the CUE facts are theorems, the zeta agreement is numerical or conditional in places, and the factorization of zeta moments into a random-matrix term and an arithmetic term is presented as a conjectural extrapolation.

units.title: An Elementary Problem Equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The v1 span includes Problem E, its divisor-sum inequality and equality case, Theorem 1.1, and the stated dependency on Robin's deeper criterion.
units.context_limit: The v0 span began after the displayed Problem E statement.
units.interpretation:
Problem E packages RH into the divisor-sum inequality sigma(n) <= H_n + exp(H_n) log(H_n), with equality only at n = 1, and Theorem 1.1 states that this problem is equivalent to RH. The unit also explains why the reformulation matters: it shifts the visible objects from zeta zeros to harmonic numbers and divisor sums.

But the source is equally explicit that the apparent elementary surface does not remove the underlying hardness. The equivalence runs through Robin's criterion and the deeper results behind it, so the mathematical operation is a representation change, not a simplification that dissolves the original difficulty.

units.title: An Elementary Problem Equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: Prime-distribution fluctuations are transferred to extremal divisor sums on a thin set, and failure of RH is predicted to yield sparse, very large counterexamples.
units.interpretation:
The span explains why RH-sensitive behavior for the divisor-sum inequality should be sought on a thin structured set rather than across all integers uniformly. Colossally abundant numbers are singled out because prime-distribution fluctuations are amplified there in the growth of sigma(n)/n. The text then contrasts the RH bound |pi(x)-Li(x)|<x^(1/2+eps) with the RH-failure scenario pi(x)>Li(x)+x^(1/2+delta) infinitely often.

The transfer from prime excess to divisor-sum excess is explicitly heuristic in this excerpt. The idea is that at heights where primes overshoot Li(x), suitable products of primes up to x with chosen exponents may produce n for which sigma(n) exceeds e^gamma n log log n. Even if RH were false, the source says the resulting counterexamples should still be very sparse and very large.

units.title: The pair correlation of zeros of the zeta function
units.selection_reason: Under an explicit RH assumption, a weighted Fourier transform probes differences between zero ordinates and proves its behavior only on a restricted frequency range.
units.interpretation:
Assuming RH, the paper studies the differences y-y' between zero ordinates through the weighted Fourier statistic F(alpha,T). The theorem states that F is real and even, and for fixed 0<=alpha<1 it has an asymptotic whose first term behaves like a Dirac mass at alpha=0 while the remaining visible term is alpha.

The nonparaphrase content is the transform itself. Instead of counting pairs directly, the span moves the spacing problem into a Fourier-side observable where the diagonal coincidence y=y' is isolated from the off-diagonal interaction. The theorem only certifies that picture on the restricted alpha range stated in the excerpt, and the whole discussion is explicitly conditional on RH.

units.title: The pair correlation of zeros of the zeta function
units.selection_reason: Extrapolation beyond the proved range yields the pair-correlation conjecture; Dyson's observation then selects the unitary/Hermitian symmetry class and rejects nearby alternatives.
units.interpretation:
Montgomery uses the proved small-alpha behavior of the form factor F(alpha) to argue that the same formula cannot persist uniformly for large alpha. He then explicitly moves from theorem to heuristic: certain large-alpha averages should be near 1, which suggests the conjectural continuation F(alpha) = 1 + O(1) on bounded intervals with alpha >= 1.

That conjectural continuation feeds the pair-correlation law and, through Dyson's comparison, selects the unitary or complex Hermitian symmetry class rather than the real-symmetric or symplectic ones. The mathematical move is classification by an extrapolated form factor, not a proof of the operator behind the zeros.

units.title: Sharp conditional bounds for moments of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This introduction states the sharp conditional moment bound and explains the key shift from one Dirichlet polynomial to many jointly controlled polynomials.
units.interpretation:
The unit states a sharp RH-conditional upper-bound theorem for zeta moments and then immediately rewrites the moment integral as an average of exp(2k log |zeta(1/2 + it)|). That identity is the conceptual hinge: the moment problem is recast as a question about the distribution of log |zeta| as t varies.

This is a genuine representation change, because the later heuristic discussion can then reason about how often log |zeta| takes given sizes instead of manipulating raw powers directly. I am not relying on the exact displayed logarithmic exponent in the theorem line, since that part of the OCR is locally ambiguous, only on the clearly readable theorem intent and exponential identity.

units.title: Sharp conditional bounds for moments of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This span gives the motivating heuristic decomposition into prime ranges and random Euler products, explaining why many correlated Dirichlet polynomials should replace a single long one.
units.interpretation:
Assuming RH, the excerpt splits log|zeta(1/2+it)| into two pieces: a prime sum that still behaves like a truncated Euler product, and a nearby-zero correction. It then says the zero term is usually O(1), is sign-favorable for upper bounds, and leaves the main variance in the prime contribution.

The representation gain comes from splitting that prime contribution into short prime ranges. Later blocks contribute less variance, so the model is not one undifferentiated Dirichlet polynomial but a stack of correlated prime blocks that can be analyzed separately.

units.title: Sharp conditional bounds for moments of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This section states Proposition 1 and Proposition 2, the two technical tools that convert RH into a flexible log|zeta| bound and precise cosine-product averages.
units.interpretation:
Under RH, Proposition 1 bounds log|zeta(1/2+it)| by the real part of a prime Dirichlet polynomial whose length x can be chosen flexibly, plus a prime-square correction and a log T / log x term. Proposition 2 then gives the averaging rule for products of cos(t log p), with the visible part of the formula saying odd exponents force cancellation.

The trainable move is a toolkit shift from the critical-line size of zeta to short prime data and parity-filtered averages. What this unit securely supports is not a finished theorem but a reusable pair of devices: adjustable prime truncation on one side, and an explicit odd-exponent vanishing rule on the other.

units.title: Sharp conditional bounds for moments of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This span defines the beta_i and G(i,j) scales, the sets T and S(j), and the structural decomposition that drives the proof of the sharp moment bound.
units.interpretation:
Harper introduces a hierarchy of scales through the parameters beta_i, the prime-block Dirichlet polynomials G(i,j), the good set T, and the bad sets S(j). The interval [T,2T] is then partitioned by the first scale at which control fails, and Lemmas 1-3 give separate exponential-integral bounds on T and on each S(j).

The mechanism is an earliest-failure decomposition. Instead of estimating the full moment where zeta is large in one shot, the proof records which prime scale first causes loss of control and prices that failure level separately before summing the layers.

units.title: Sharp conditional bounds for moments of the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This section adapts the moment method from zeta to quadratic Dirichlet L-functions, showing that the many-polynomial strategy is not specific to the Riemann zeta function.
units.interpretation:
Harper explicitly adapts the zeta moment method to quadratic Dirichlet L-functions. The span states the GRH-conditional moment bound, replaces the zeta inputs by Propositions 3 and 4, and uses quadratic reciprocity to rewrite the prime sum in the discriminant variable.

The source-specific gain is that prime squares stop fluctuating and contribute a fixed half-log-log term. The transfer is therefore localized to reciprocity, orthogonality, and the simpler square contribution, not just a generic reuse of the same method.

units.title: On the value-distribution of the Riemann zeta-function on the critical line
units.selection_reason: Theorems 1 and 2 count zeta values on a fixed ray from the origin and give the first and second discrete moments that explain directional bias on the critical line.
units.interpretation:
The span samples zeta on the critical line by angle rather than by size. Theorem 1 counts the times t for which zeta(1/2+it) lies on a fixed ray e^(i phi)R, and under RH or an almost-all-critical-line hypothesis that count asymptotically matches the critical-line zero count. Theorem 2 then forms first and second discrete moments over exactly those ray-hit times.

This representation exposes directional information that ordinary magnitude statistics suppress. The first discrete moment depends on phi and even vanishes at phi=pi/2, while the leading second-moment term is independent of phi. So the operation is to convert value distribution into directional counting plus moments, separating angle-sensitive bias from angle-insensitive second-order size.

units.title: On the value-distribution of the Riemann zeta-function on the critical line
units.selection_reason: Corollaries 3 and 4 interpret the first-moment formula geometrically, identify ray-dependent mean values on zeta(1/2+iR), and show that every ray in the right half-plane contains arbitrarily large critical-line values.
units.context_limit: A later figure is referenced for illustration only; the corollaries and their interpretation are self-contained in prose.
units.interpretation:
The corollaries reorganize critical-line values by direction in the complex plane. For each ray e^{i phi}R, the source states a directional mean value, identifies the conditional mean as e^{i phi} cos phi, and singles out the purely imaginary case as unconditional.

The second move is largeness on the same representation. Every ray in the right half-plane is shown to contain arbitrarily large values, so the same directional picture controls both average behavior and extreme behavior instead of treating size alone as the only observable.

units.title: Zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions
units.selection_reason: The introduction states fixed-point and interval nonvanishing theorems for Dirichlet L-functions and explains the paper's direct-count mollifier integral in place of a moments argument.
units.interpretation:
The span makes its own novelty explicit: it aims to count characters with the desired nonvanishing property directly, rather than reaching them through moments of L-functions. To do that it introduces a Barban-Vehov mollifier whose associated coefficients a(n) vanish on an initial range, and it studies one contour integral that can be expanded both as a Dirichlet sum and as L(s, chi)M(s, chi) plus a shifted integral.

That setup turns pointwise nonvanishing into a family-level counting mechanism. The fixed-point theorem and the interval theorem use the same device, but the excerpt also marks the boundary between them: for the interval result the choice of Y matters and is taken to be a power of q, whereas for the fixed-point result the source says the choice is much less delicate.

units.title: Zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions
units.selection_reason: Section 11 proves positive-proportion nonvanishing at a fixed point by balancing mollified first- and second-moment estimates and converting them into a count of characters with L(a, chi) not equal to zero.
units.context_limit: Normalized formulas are extraction-noisy, but the fixed-point nonvanishing mechanism and proportion bound are supported by readable prose.
units.interpretation:
Theorem 11.1 claims that for fixed 1/2 <= a < 1 and sufficiently large prime q, a positive proportion of characters mod q satisfy L(a,chi) != 0. The proof does not search for nonvanishing character by character. Instead it forms a mollified quantity S(s0,chi), splits the characters according to whether L(s0,chi)=0, and combines earlier first- and second-moment estimates with Cauchy-Schwarz.

The key mechanism is indirect extraction. A large mollified first moment and a controlled second moment cannot both hold unless many characters contribute from the nonvanishing side, so the count of nonzero L-values is recovered from the moment comparison rather than from pointwise analysis.

units.title: Zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions
units.selection_reason: Section 12 upgrades fixed-point nonvanishing to a whole interval by covering the strip with short intervals and applying Cauchy's theorem to count characters whose L-functions avoid real zeros.
units.context_limit: Readable prose supports the interval-covering and Cauchy-integral mechanism despite formula-extraction noise.
units.interpretation:
The theorem upgrades nonvanishing from one fixed real point to an entire real segment in the critical strip. The proof covers the segment by intervals of length 1/log q, chooses a representative point in an interval containing a real zero, surrounds the interval center by a small circle, and uses Cauchy's theorem to convert the existence of a zero into a contour integral that can be averaged over characters.

The gain is uniformity by localization. Real-zero detection is replaced by a short-interval covering plus local contour counts, while the exceptional near-1 range with at most one real zero is explicitly set aside rather than absorbed into the main mechanism.

Assuming RH, Spira reflects the derivative-zero question to the logarithmic derivative at 1-s by the functional equation and then inserts a partial-fraction expansion. In that reflected form each zeta zero contributes a positive real-part term, so the zero set becomes a barrier rather than an uncontrolled oscillatory contribution.

The excerpt then bounds the gamma and tangent terms and drives the comparison to a large-|s| sign estimate. What this span actually supplies is the large-height exclusion step for 0 < Re(s) < 1/2; it is part of a broader theorem rather than a self-contained proof for every height.

units.title: Zeros of $\zeta^{\prime} (s)$ and the Riemann hypothesis

Only after that does the monotonicity consequence appear. In the indicated regions, RH yields leftward increase of absolute zeta prime, but the exact formulas and sign bookkeeping are inherited and partly OCR-blurred, so the safe object here is the region-specific reformulation, not a clean standalone equivalence theorem.

units.title: Equivalence of Riesz and Baez-Duarte criterion for the Riemann Hypothesis
units.selection_reason: The theorem converts decay of c_k into growth bounds for R(x) through the exponential generating function, making the Riesz and Baez-Duarte criteria equivalent up to the deferred reverse implication.

units.interpretation:
This excerpt proves only one direction of the advertised equivalence. Assuming c_k = O(k^(-delta)), it invokes a Polya-Szego asymptotic for weighted power-series coefficients and specializes it to a_k = 1/k! so that sum k^(-delta) x^k / k! behaves like x^(-delta) e^x.

That weighted asymptotic is then inserted into the exponential generating relation between c_k and R(x), turning discrete decay of the coefficients into the growth bound R(x) = O(x^(1-delta)). The mathematical object is the discrete-to-continuous bridge itself; the reverse implication is explicitly outside the span.

units.title: Equivalence of Riesz and Baez-Duarte criterion for the Riemann Hypothesis

The introduction places the Riesz function R(x) and the Baez-Duarte sequence c_k side by side as two RH criteria with different visible forms: one is a continuous growth problem and the other a discrete decay problem. It then states that the paper will not stop at transitivity through RH, but will relate the two criteria directly.

The trainable object is the exponent bookkeeping. The source proposes the more general equivalence c_k=O(k^{-delta}) iff R(x)=O(x^{1-delta}), so the continuous and discrete formulations are treated as two representations of the same decay-versus-growth balance.

units.title: Critical zeros of the Riemann zeta-function

That makes the unit an admissibility analysis of the mollifier architecture rather than a bare score report.
