In this unit that covariance structure is a motivating bridge, not a standalone proof: it explains why the authors compare maxima of zeta on short intervals with maxima of random-matrix models, while the theorem itself is only presented at leading order here.

units.title: Maximum of the Riemann Zeta Function on a Short Interval of the Critical Line
units.selection_reason: The authors explain the three-step reduction from short-interval zeta maxima to blockwise Dirichlet polynomials and sketch why branching-random-walk ideas become relevant for the lower bound.
units.interpretation:
For the lower bound in the short-interval maximum theorem, the paper first moves from log|zeta(1/2+iu)| to values of zeta slightly right of the critical line, where a mollifier M(s) can be built so that zeta(s)M(s) is approximately 1 for most t. That reduction turns the problem into the study of a prime Dirichlet polynomial over p<=X. The next step splits the primes into blocks J_j chosen so that the block sums have comparable variance and asymptotic independence.

The logic is representation selection before estimation. A hard zeta maximum is replaced by a multiscale prime field that can be analyzed with branching-random-walk methods, so the proof route depends on changing the object, not on attacking the original form head-on.

units.title: Maximum of the Riemann Zeta Function on a Short Interval of the Critical Line
units.selection_reason: Lemma 4.1 shows that, with high probability, a large value of zeta slightly to the right of the critical line propagates into a large value on the critical line, supplying the first step of Proposition 3.1.
units.interpretation:
Lemma 4.1 compares large values slightly to the right of the critical line with large values on the critical line itself. The proof writes zeta(sigma+it) as a Poisson-type average of critical-line values, then shows by Cauchy-Schwarz and mean-square estimates that the exceptional set where the off-line maximum is large but the critical-line maximum stays small has measure o(T).

The mechanism is harmonic transfer of extreme events. Largeness in a very thin right-hand strip survives the averaging kernel unless too much mass hides in remote tails, and the source proves that this tail-hiding scenario is statistically negligible.

units.title: Some remarks on the mean value of the Riemann zeta-function and other Dirichlet series 1
units.selection_reason: The selected unit states the general L-series mean-value theorem and immediately explains the Cauchy-integral mechanism used to deduce it from the preceding maximal bound theorem.
units.interpretation:
The deduction rewrites the target quantity F(s)=L(s) through Cauchy's theorem as an integral over a rectangle with corners on the lines u=1/2, u=2, and the short t-range under study. The source then isolates which parts of that contour matter by saying the horizontal edges and the line u=2 contribute only bounded quantities when the parameter b is chosen large.

The mechanism supported by this span is therefore contour relocation, not a general story about critical-line transfer. A short-interval mean-value statement is reduced to a boundary integral in selected parameter cases, with the Galois and non-Galois hypotheses entering through earlier conditions rather than being rederived here.

units.title: Some remarks on the mean value of the Riemann zeta-function and other Dirichlet series 1
units.selection_reason: Collects the auxiliary lemmas that control logarithmic derivatives and zero contributions in the main mean-value analysis.
units.interpretation:
The density estimate is organized as a detector, block, and moment pipeline. Lemma 4 starts by selecting a well-spaced zero system and estimating its size with the zero-detecting function F(s) M_H(s)-1, Lemma 5 sharpens the count farther to the right, and the interval is then partitioned into good and bad blocks according to nearby zeros.

The good blocks are where the moment calculation happens, while bad blocks are discarded because their total length is small. OCR damage prevents trustworthy reconstruction of every exponent and parameter, but the proof architecture itself is clear and source-specific.

units.title: Some remarks on the mean value of the Riemann zeta-function and other Dirichlet series 1
units.selection_reason: States and proves the fallback mean-value theorem that survives after dropping the Euler-product assumption, making the paper's transfer principle more robust.
units.interpretation:
This theorem drops the Euler product and replaces it with two other controls: a coefficient-growth hypothesis and a lower bound on |F(2 eta)| as eta tends to 0 from the right. Under those stronger assumptions, the source states a lower bound for the mean value Q(1) over a vertical interval.

The mechanism is that boundary growth near the real axis substitutes for the missing multiplicative structure. The proof sketch reduces the claim to a lower bound on max Q(sigma) and begins a contradiction argument near sigma=1, while explicitly noting both that the hypotheses are stronger than necessary and that the proof is only sketched.

units.title: Moments of zeta and correlations of divisor-sums: IV
units.selection_reason: The core theorem identifies the convolution analogue of the shifted divisor sum and explains the new M,N splitting of m1m2 - n1n2 = h into two linear relations.
units.context_limit: Residue notation and the arithmetic factors D_A, D_B, and B(.,.) are defined earlier.
units.interpretation:
The notable feature of this span is the appearance of the extra M, N summation in the convolution identity. The source explains that these parameters arise by splitting the nonlinear constraint m1 m2 - n1 n2 = h into two linear shifted equations, Mm1 - Nn1 = h1 and Nm2 - Mn2 = h2, while keeping m1/n1 and n2/m2 close to M/N.

That is the conceptual mechanism, not just heavier notation. A multiplicative difference is decomposed into two coupled linear constraints organized by a rational-approximation parameter, which is why the paper likens the calculation to a circle-method argument.

units.title: Moments of zeta and correlations of divisor-sums: IV
units.selection_reason: This span begins the paper’s second major mechanism by setting up the Type II convolution sums that will later account for the higher-swap terms in the moment calculation.
units.context_limit: Depends on the shifted-divisor notation and set partitions A,B introduced earlier.
units.interpretation:
The unit rewrites tau_A and tau_B as convolutions and introduces the Type II off-diagonal sum over m1,m2,n1,n2 with m1m2 close to n1n2. It then applies a discrete circle-method setup: approximate m1/n1 by a Farey fraction M/N, define h1=m1N-n1M and h2=m2M-n2N, and rewrite both the difference m1m2-n1n2 and the logarithm of the ratio n1n2/(m1m2) in terms of h1/(m1N), h2/(m2M), and a negligible error.

The source-specific gain is that multiplicative near-equality becomes a pair of small additive defects. Once that translation is made, the off-diagonal can be reorganized by M,N,h1,h2 and treated structurally rather than as one dense multiplicative condition.

units.title: Moments of zeta and correlations of divisor-sums: IV
units.selection_reason: This span explains why the correlation-side combinatorics overcount the recipe terms and shows that divisor-factor automorphisms exactly account for the multiplicity.
units.context_limit: Uses the decompositions m=m1m2, n=n1n2 and the earlier split A=A1∪A2, B=B1∪B2.
units.interpretation:
The final step explains apparent overcounting by identifying real automorphisms of the shifted-correlation parameterization. Factorizations of m_i and n_i generate transformed variables that preserve the same paired linear system, and counting these automorphisms gives exactly the same multiplicity as the number of admissible decompositions on the recipe side.

So the multiplicity is intrinsic symmetry, not a mistake. Once the representation is quotiented by that symmetry, each swap term survives exactly once and the two combinatorial descriptions agree.

units.title: An exponentially-smoothed Gram-type formula for the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This span compares Gram, Riemann-Siegel, and smoothed formulas, then explains why the generalized incomplete-gamma smoothing still forces an O(t) cutoff and hence a Gram-type expansion.
units.interpretation:
The span compares three truncation regimes for zeta computation: Gram's O(t) cutoff, the shorter Riemann-Siegel cutoff near sqrt(t), and smoothed formulas built from complementary-error or incomplete-gamma factors. Its key point is that simple smoothing removes the sharp cutoff discontinuity but does not preserve the short cutoff once one demands asymptotic control of the correction and remainder terms.

So the mathematics here is a tradeoff analysis, not a generic praise of smoothing. The source says that the asymptotic bookkeeping forces the smoothed main sum back to O(t) terms, which means the resulting formula remains Gram-type rather than genuinely Riemann-Siegel-type.

units.title: An exponentially-smoothed Gram-type formula for the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This section derives the generalized smoothed expansion for xi(s) using Mellin inversion of the incomplete gamma function and shows how the new formula extends the earlier special case.
units.interpretation:
The expansion starts by replacing a sharp cutoff with incomplete-gamma smoothing. Mellin inversion of Gamma(a,x) turns the smoothed Dirichlet series into a Perron-type integral, and contour shifts across z=0 and z=1-s generate explicit residue terms.

The resulting representation writes zeta(s) as a smoothed Dirichlet series plus correction terms whose coefficients A_m involve shifted zeta values. Exponential smoothing and residue calculus systematically unfold correction structure that a hard truncation would hide.

units.title: An exponentially-smoothed Gram-type formula for the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This span isolates the remainder term and proves the usable bound on R_M, which is essential for judging when the smoothed expansion is computationally meaningful.
units.interpretation:
The excerpt attacks the remainder term R_M by changing its representation rather than estimating the original contour integral directly. After applying the functional relation and a change of variables, the remainder is rewritten in terms of an integral involving a gamma-function ratio F(y) and a scaled monotone version G_p(M;y).

That new form is computationally useful because monotonicity and Stirling input make incomplete-gamma bounds available. The final result is an explicit bound on |R_M| in terms of gamma factors, zeta(M+1-a+delta), exponential decay in t, and the auxiliary factor C_p(M;t).

units.title: An exponentially-smoothed Gram-type formula for the Riemann zeta function
units.selection_reason: This section specializes to exponential smoothing and explains why the main sum still has a Gram-type cutoff, including the optimal-truncation and accuracy tradeoffs in p and K.
units.interpretation:
With a=1, the main Dirichlet sum acquires the exponential smoothing factor exp[-(n/K)^(2p)]. The source then studies the correction series and shows that its terms have asymptotic character only if K>t/(2 pi). That requirement forces the effective cutoff n* to stay at Gram scale rather than at the shorter Riemann-Siegel scale. The unit goes on to discuss the optimal truncation index M0 and how increasing p both improves the decay of the smoothed main sum and worsens the eventual asymptotic behavior of the correction series.

This is a tradeoff audit, not a free smoothing trick. Exponential smoothing does simplify the main sum, but the correction series imposes a hidden cost that fixes the cutoff length and limits the accuracy gains available from larger p.

units.title: On mean value results for the Riemann zeta-function in short intervals.
units.selection_reason: This section treats the sigma > 1 case by expanding zeta^k, separating diagonal from off-diagonal terms, and deriving the short-interval asymptotic I_sigma(T+H,k)-I_sigma(T,k)=C(k,sigma)H+O(1).
units.interpretation:
For sigma>1 the span expands zeta(s)^k into its Dirichlet series with coefficients d_k(n), inserts that expansion into the 2k-th moment integral, and splits the resulting double sum into diagonal terms m=n and non-diagonal terms m!=n. The diagonal terms contribute the main constant C(k,sigma), while the off-diagonal terms are shown to stay bounded after integration.

The operative mechanism is phase averaging after a representation change. Once the moment is rewritten as a double Dirichlet sum, the coherent diagonal survives as the main term and the oscillatory non-diagonal part loses enough coherence to contribute only O(1). The span also states the scope clearly: this is the only easy case, and it is restricted to fixed k and sigma>1.

units.title: On mean value results for the Riemann zeta-function in short intervals.
units.selection_reason: States the principal asymptotic formulas in the easier half-plane regimes, clarifying what changes before the critical-strip case.
units.interpretation:
The strip 1/2<sigma<1 already exhibits layered moment asymptotics. The mean square has a main term, an explicit T^(2-2 sigma) secondary term, and an error E_sigma(T); the fourth moment has its own main term, and for 1/2<sigma<3/4 the source adds still more lower-order main terms with a separate error E_2(T,sigma).

The structural lesson is that the moment expansion becomes richer as sigma moves left toward the critical line. Terms that are negligible near sigma=1 become mathematically necessary in thinner parts of the strip, and the source even notes where a nominal error can dominate one displayed lower-order term.

units.title: On mean value results for the Riemann zeta-function in short intervals.
units.selection_reason: Relates the remainder exponent to the critical infimum sigma_k^*, which is the conceptual hinge between the moment problem and zeta growth.
units.interpretation:
The span compares two different remainder bounds for the same mean-value problem and says when each one is useful. Bound 4.9 is better when sigma is near 1, while bound 4.10 is better when sigma is near sigma_k star, and the text immediately converts those abstract exponents into example asymptotics for sixth, eighth, and tenth moments.

So the move is deliberate perspective selection inside an estimate. The proof keeps both control parameters available and splices them according to where each dominates.

units.title: On mean value results for the Riemann zeta-function in short intervals.
units.selection_reason: Develops the RH-conditional measure estimate that sharpens the critical-strip moment bound and explains the source of the improved exponent.
units.interpretation:
Assuming RH, the proof sketch says that a large value of log|zeta(1/2+it)| must force one of two truncated prime sums to be large: S_1 from the smaller primes or S_2 from the next range. The event of a large zeta value is therefore reduced to one of two more concrete witness events.

The rest of the argument is regime selection. Measures mu_1 and mu_2 are attached to those witness events, high moments are estimated with Lemma 3, and the parameters A and r are chosen differently in three V-ranges, so the bound is assembled by matching the right witness to the right scale.

units.title: Mean values of L-functions and symmetry
units.selection_reason: This passage identifies the symplectic symmetry family, lists its model L-function families, records the conjectured moment asymptotics, and extracts the corresponding symmetry parameter B(k).
units.interpretation:
The passage groups several arithmetic families under the symplectic symmetry label by using their conjectured moment growth as the organizing invariant. Quadratic Dirichlet characters, symmetric-square families, and the listed twisted families are presented as different instances with the same exponent pattern.

The compression step is the point. Family-specific averages are replaced by shared symmetry data, recorded here as V(z)=z and B(k)=1/2 k(k+1), while the parameter A is deferred to the same procedure used for orthogonal families. The unit is conjectural throughout, but the symmetry-type abstraction is explicit.

units.title: Mean values of L-functions and symmetry
units.selection_reason: Gives the orthogonal-family moment conjecture and the corresponding symmetry parameter, forming a direct conceptual complement to the covered symplectic case.
units.interpretation:
The span proposes a common moment law for orthogonal families of L-functions ordered by conductor: central values should average like a_k g_k (log QA)^{B(k)} / Gamma(1+B(k)). For the orthogonal examples listed, the source identifies V(z)=z and B(k)=k(k-1)/2, records small values of g_k from earlier work, and notes that the families split into even and odd subfamilies, with the odd central values vanishing identically.

The abstraction is symmetry through moment growth. Different families are compressed into one orthogonal type not by sharing the same coefficients, but by sharing the same central-moment exponent and parity structure.

units.title: Mean values of L-functions and symmetry
units.selection_reason: Packages the Barnes double-gamma factorization that explains the pole structure governing the conjectural moment constants.
units.interpretation:
Theorem 4.1 organizes the constants g_lambda by the meromorphic anatomy of g_lambda/Gamma(1+B(lambda)). For the unitary, orthogonal, and symplectic cases it lists exact pole orders, says the function never vanishes, and treats these pole patterns as the invariant to be explained. Corollary 4.2 then packages the constants with ordinary Gamma and Barnes-Vigneras double-Gamma factors and relates the three symmetry types.

The move is compression by special-function factorization. Rather than handling each family of constants separately, the source identifies one meromorphic pattern and lets the Barnes double-Gamma function carry that pattern.

units.title: Mean values of L-functions and symmetry
units.selection_reason: Develops the arithmetic integrality and recursion properties of g_k, turning the symmetry constants into a coherent number-theoretic object.
units.interpretation:
Theorem 5.1 demystifies the symmetry constants g_k by turning them into finite products with readable valuations. Lemma 5.2 rewrites the unitary, orthogonal, and symplectic constants as factorial and double-factorial products, after which p-adic nonnegativity becomes a counting problem instead of a mysterious analytic fact.

The result is stronger than saying the constants are integers. The theorem also specifies when v_p(g_k)=0 and tracks the orthogonal and symplectic cases separately.

units.title: Mean values of L-functions and symmetry
units.selection_reason: Introduces the piecewise self-similar valuation function that organizes denominator growth and links the constants to a fractal-style arithmetic pattern.
units.interpretation:
Theorems 6.1 and 6.2 package several p-adic valuation asymptotics into a single profile function c_p(x). Along the sequence k_j=[p^j x], the valuations of multiple arithmetic objects grow proportionally to c_p(x), so one real-variable function carries the asymptotic data.

The second theorem turns arithmetic congruence into local geometry of that function. Near rational points a/b, c_p(x) is classified as self-similar, cusped, or vertically tangent depending on congruence conditions, so residue-class information is recoded as singularity type.

units.title: Low lying zeros of families of L-functions
units.selection_reason: This span defines the one-level density, lists the symmetry densities, formulates the density conjecture, and states the main theorem for GL2 and symmetric-square families.
units.interpretation:
The source defines the one-level density D(F, phi) by scaling ordinates of zeros near 1/2 by log conductor, averaging that statistic over a family ordered by conductor, and comparing the result to explicit candidate densities for orthogonal and symplectic symmetry types. The theorem then states orthogonal limits for the listed GL2-related families under GRH and the support restriction on phi-hat.

The operation is to compress an entire family of zero sets into one observable that can be matched against a symmetry template. The boundary matters: conductor scaling and compact Fourier support are part of what the theorem actually controls, rather than incidental packaging.

units.title: Low lying zeros of families of L-functions
units.selection_reason: This corollary turns the one-level density statements into concrete lower bounds for nonvanishing in several families, which is a separate extraction target from the theorem statement itself.
units.interpretation:
Assuming GRH for the relevant GL2 and Dirichlet L-functions, Corollary 2 gives explicit lower bounds for nonvanishing proportions in several families, including values above 9/16, 15/16, and 55/64, and it also bounds average order of vanishing in another family. The remarks then explain what these numbers are spending: without the support extension in Theorem 1, the method would stall at the older lower bound of at least 1/2.

The unit is therefore about converting one-level density into explicit proportions only after enough Fourier support has been won. The extra support is not cosmetic; it is the exact resource that moves the output beyond the baseline half-nonvanishing barrier.

units.title: Low lying zeros of families of L-functions
units.selection_reason: This span introduces the weighted averaging operator, states the support-extension hypothesis, and explains the striking quasi-RH consequence for GL2 L-functions once the support exceeds (-2,2).
units.interpretation:
Theorem 3 gives the orthogonal one-level density for the weighted average A_K when the Fourier support of the test function lies in (-2,2). The paper then introduces Hypothesis 4, a cancellation statement for analytic exponential sums over primes in progressions, and under that hypothesis extends the support to (-7/3,7/3). Corollary 6 adds a further consequence: assuming both Hypothesis 4 and the stated auxiliary restriction on possible zero locations, sufficiently large-weight forms have no zeros with beta>13/14.

The source shows that wider Fourier support increases what one-level density can enforce. The result is still conditional and the extra zero-location assumption must stay visible, but the mechanism is concrete: extending support strengthens the statistic from symmetry identification toward a restricted zero-exclusion statement.

units.title: Low lying zeros of families of L-functions
units.selection_reason: This calculation is where the off-diagonal terms stop being error and instead create the orthogonal main term that distinguishes the even and odd sign subfamilies.
units.interpretation:
The second term in equation 50 becomes a main term only after two representation changes. The source first rewrites it using Kloosterman sums and character expansions, then invokes GRH for Dirichlet L-functions so that nonprincipal characters contribute only error while the principal character survives.

That separation reveals the hidden main term. What looked off-diagonal and secondary becomes a principal-character contribution with explicit weight, and the Kloosterman algebra is part of the extraction rather than dispensable detail.

units.title: Low lying zeros of families of L-functions
units.selection_reason: This span begins the symmetric-square family analysis and sets up the decomposition that leads to the symplectic one-level density, giving a genuinely different family behavior from the GL2 parity split.
units.interpretation:
For the symmetric-square family, the explicit formula converts low-lying zeros into an integral term together with prime sums involving Hecke eigenvalues. The family average S_K[D_K(F,phi)] is then set up so that the limiting statistic can be read from the averaged prime-coefficient expressions.

The goal is family classification by kernel rather than coefficient-by-coefficient description. Under GRH and the support restriction on phi-hat, the target main term is the symplectic one-level density kernel 1-sin(2pi x)/(2pi x), so the family is identified by the universal statistic its averaged explicit formula tends toward.

units.title: Riemann zeta fractional derivative—functional equation and link with primes
units.selection_reason: This theorem-level span links the fractional derivative zeta^(alpha) to a prime-indexed series in the left half-plane and explains the prime-distribution interpretation.
units.interpretation:
The paper begins by saying that the zero theory of zeta^(alpha) is too weak to support a critical-line story for fractional derivatives. Rather than pretend otherwise, the span changes representation and asks what prime-information content survives in a half-plane where the manipulations are legal.

Theorem 4.3 answers that by linking zeta^(alpha)(s) for Re(s) < 0 to a prime-power double series, with the weak equivalence that the two sides converge or diverge together. The operative move is to trade an unavailable zero picture for an Euler-product-style prime expansion.

units.title: Riemann zeta fractional derivative—functional equation and link with primes
units.selection_reason: This span explains why the original fractional derivative is computationally unusable and replaces it with the forward Grünwald-Letnikov derivative that still reproduces zeta^(alpha).
units.interpretation:
The paper drops the original fractional derivative because it is bad both for deriving a functional equation and for computation. It replaces that operator with the forward Grunwald-Letnikov derivative, whose generalized Leibniz rule recovers the Dirichlet-series formula zeta^(alpha)(s)=e^(i pi alpha) sum_{n>=2} log^alpha(n)/n^s for real alpha. The source then writes the resulting functional equation as a large multi-index expansion involving Gamma derivatives and ordinary zeta derivatives.

The lesson is split capability. The new derivative repairs algebraic manipulability on the Dirichlet-series side, but it does not repair computational usability on the functional-equation side: the paper says numerical approximations of the new formula still overflow buffers.

units.title: Riemann zeta fractional derivative—functional equation and link with primes
units.selection_reason: This section derives Theorem 3.3, reducing the original high-cost functional equation to a single infinite series and making the fractional analogue computationally tractable.
units.interpretation:
Proposition 3.1 rewrites the derivative side of zeta's functional equation in terms of complex exponentials multiplying derivatives of Gamma(1-s)zeta(1-s). Lemma 3.2 then computes the fractional derivative of e^((1-s)w) explicitly, and Theorem 3.3 combines these ingredients into a single-series functional equation for zeta^(alpha)(s).

The representation gain is diagonalization by exponentials. Once the costly part of the functional equation is written in a basis on which fractional differentiation acts directly, the fractional analogue becomes a one-series computation rather than a more tangled symbolic object.

units.title: Riemann zeta fractional derivative—functional equation and link with primes
units.selection_reason: This theorem develops the symmetric-form analogue T_alpha(s) .= T_alpha(1-s), which is conceptually different from the simplified one-series formula and frames the fractional theory as a functional equation.
units.interpretation:
The fractional derivative is made compatible with zeta's reflection symmetry by distributing derivative order across the completed factors. Lemma 3.5 computes D^alpha zeta(1-s)=e^(-i pi alpha) zeta^(alpha)(1-s), and Theorem 3.6 then packages ordinary derivatives of Gamma and zeta into T_alpha(s), which is symmetric under s and 1-s up to multiplicative constant.

The point is that one cannot just fractionally differentiate a single side of the functional equation and expect symmetry to survive. The paper restores that symmetry by building a completed combination whose pieces share the derivative burden.

units.title: Riemann zeta fractional derivative—functional equation and link with primes
units.selection_reason: This span rewrites eta^(alpha) and the strip series in terms of zeta^(alpha), giving the bridge that connects the fractional zeta derivatives back to the alternating series and strip geometry.
units.interpretation:
Theorem 4.1 starts from eta(s)=zeta(s)(1-2^{1-s}) and applies fractional differentiation to that identity. For noninteger alpha, eta^(alpha)(s) and the related logarithmically weighted strip series are both rewritten as infinite combinations of fractional zeta derivatives weighted by powers of log 2.

The bridge is therefore operational rather than rhetorical. Alternating-series information is transported into zeta language by a generalized Leibniz rule, and Corollary 4.2 records the special simplification that the infinite expansion truncates when alpha is an integer.

units.title: Multiple Dirichlet Series and Moments of Zeta and L -Functions
units.selection_reason: The main theorem gives cubic-moment asymptotics from multiple Dirichlet series and immediately highlights the expected extra pole at w=3/4 as the next analytic obstacle.
units.interpretation:
The theorem gives weighted and unweighted cubic-moment asymptotics with a degree-six polynomial in log x and a sharper error term, while also saying the weighted version shows the best error obtainable by the present method. The span then explains that the same multiple-Dirichlet-series framework should recover all coefficients of the main polynomial.

What remains tentative is also stated in the source. The authors expect an additional simple pole at w=3/4 for Z(1/2,1/2,1/2,w), but they do not claim it here as established fact. So the unit supports a bookkeeping role for the higher-dimensional series and an explicitly marked possible refinement, not a proven extra mechanism.

units.title: Multiple Dirichlet Series and Moments of Zeta and L -Functions
units.selection_reason: Section 2.1 defines the zeta multiple Dirichlet series, proves Proposition 2.1 on its continuation, and introduces Lemma 2.2 to control the oscillatory integral that isolates the pole at w equals 1.
units.interpretation:
The source defines multiple Dirichlet series Z_{E_1,...,E_{2m};k}(s_1,...,s_{2m};w) by integrating a product of shifted zeta-functions against the oscillatory factor (2 pi e / t)^(k i t) t^-w. Proposition 2.1 gives continuation into wider domains and shows that when k=0 there is a single simple pole at w=1. Lemma 2.2 isolates the model oscillatory integral I_{B;k}(w), proving its continuation and identifying I_{1;0}(w)=1/(w-1).

The analytic hazard is deliberately concentrated into one scalar kernel. Once the behavior of I_{B;k}(w) is understood, the continuation and pole structure of the larger multi-zeta object become manageable rather than diffuse across all variables.

units.title: A strengthening of the Nyman-Beurling criterion for the Riemann hypothesis, 2
units.selection_reason: This span states the strengthened Nyman-Beurling criterion chi in B_nat, explains why the standard approximants are inadequate, and introduces the corrective fs(x) construction.
units.interpretation:
The span strengthens the Nyman-Beurling criterion by replacing membership of chi in the large space B with membership in the thinner space B_nat. It then explains why the standard finite approximants F_n and the Selberg-style mollified approximants are inadequate in H, and introduces the family f_s(x) = sum mu(a) rho_a(x) / a^s as an all-scales substitute.

The conceptual gain is that f_s uses the whole range of a at once instead of betting on a single slow finite cutoff. The source explicitly describes f_s as a sort of correction of 1/zeta(s), and it keeps the boundary clear: membership f_epsilon in B_nat is proved under RH, while H-convergence to -chi is stated unconditionally.

units.title: A strengthening of the Nyman-Beurling criterion for the Riemann hypothesis, 2
units.selection_reason: These lemmas import the Balazard-Saias approximation and the zeta-ratio bound that make the strengthened Nyman-Beurling argument work in Hilbert-space norm rather than only pointwise.
units.interpretation:
The strengthened Nyman-Beurling argument begins with two safeguards. The first lemma imports zero-free information by showing that a truncated Mobius series approximates 1/zeta(s) uniformly in a right half-plane if zeta has no zeros there. The second lemma is unconditional and bounds the ratio zeta(1/2-epsilon+i tau)/zeta(1/2+epsilon+i tau), preventing reflection across the critical line from introducing uncontrolled growth.

Together these lemmas move the criterion from raw pointwise identities toward Hilbert-space control. One gives a finite approximation where zero-free information is available; the other guarantees that reflecting the problem does not destroy the needed norms.

units.title: A strengthening of the Nyman-Beurling criterion for the Riemann hypothesis, 2
units.selection_reason: This span is the proof proper: it defines f_{epsilon,n}, moves to the Fourier-Mellin transform, and proves convergence in H to -chi under RH.
units.interpretation:
The proof of the RH implies Nyman-Beurling direction works by moving the approximation problem into Fourier-Mellin space. The source defines Mobius-weighted approximants f_{epsilon,n}, identifies their pointwise limits, and then uses the isometry M to rewrite X_epsilon f_{2 epsilon,n} as a zeta quotient times a partial Mobius sum.

In that representation the convergence problem becomes analytic control of the quotient. Littlewood's theorem and RH-implied Lindelof bounds provide that control, first as n tends to infinity and then as epsilon tends to 0, yielding convergence in the relevant Hilbert norm.

units.title: A strengthening of the Nyman-Beurling criterion for the Riemann hypothesis, 2
units.selection_reason: This proposition extracts a quantitative approximating sequence with explicit (log log n)^(-1/3) decay, which is a separate constructive payoff from the equivalence theorem itself.
units.interpretation:
Proposition 3.1 turns an abstract Nyman-Beurling closure statement into a quantitative approximating family. Instead of a raw Mobius truncation, the source inserts an analytic weight depending on log a/log log n and obtains an RH-conditional H-distance to chi of order (log log n)^(-1/3).

The repair works because the Fourier-Mellin transform converts that H-distance into an integral involving ratios of zeta-values. Once the integral is split and controlled by Burnol's estimate and the Balazard-Saias lemma, the analytically weighted family becomes a concrete summability substitute for a failing finite cutoff.

units.title: A small improvement in the gaps between consecutive zeros of the Riemann zeta-function
units.selection_reason: Preobrazhenskii states the improved conditional bounds on mu and lambda and introduces the h(c) coefficient test and historical coefficient choices that convert chosen sequences a_k into zero-gap estimates.
units.context_limit: The proof and optimized coefficient choices occur later in the paper.
units.interpretation:
The span turns large and small zero-gap bounds into a test-functional problem. Under RH, one defines h(c) from a coefficient sequence a_k, and the Montgomery-Odlyzko criterion then says that h(c) < 1 forces lambda >= c while h(c) > 1 forces mu <= c. The source packages the new numerical bounds through that sign test.

So the gap question is not attacked by locating individual zeros directly. It is bridged to the design of coefficients inside an explicit formula criterion, with the sign of h(c) - 1 acting as the switch between information about large gaps and information about small gaps.

units.title: A small improvement in the gaps between consecutive zeros of the Riemann zeta-function
units.selection_reason: This span explains the specific mollifier-style coefficient choice used to improve the gap bounds and records the intrinsic limits of the Montgomery–Odlyzko method that prevent reaching μ=1/2.

units.title: Farey series and the Riemann hypothesis

The concrete mechanism is an explicit asymptotic comparison. Because x^(-b) eventually dominates x^(-1/2) when b<1/2, the RH-failure lower bound is incompatible with the proposed upper bound 2/sqrt(x) for log f(x). This is therefore a conditional contradiction lemma about one auxiliary function, not a full equivalence or an independent proof program in the excerpt.

units.title: Currently there are no reasons to doubt the Riemann Hypothesis: The zeta function beyond the realm of computation

units.title: Scalar modular bootstrap and zeros of the Riemann zeta function

If every zero has real part 1/2, the whole oscillatory sector scales like T^(c/2 - 3/4); a zero farther right would enlarge that subsubleading term. The representation gain is precise: a zero-distribution claim becomes a bound on the size of a CFT asymptotic correction.

units.title: Scalar modular bootstrap and zeros of the Riemann zeta function

The scalar part of the crossing equation is rewritten as a sum over scalar conformal weights plus vacuum terms and an s-integral. The contour in s is then moved to the right of c/2, and the source states that the enclosed poles are at s=c/2 and at points built from the nontrivial zeta zeros, namely (1+z_n)/2 and z_n/2. The resulting formula expresses the scalar crossing relation as vacuum pieces, a moduli-dependent epsilon_c(mu) term, a sum over k with exponents controlled by zeta zeros, and a remaining vertical integral.

The transformation is residue-based. A modular crossing identity is converted into a sum rule whose oscillatory exponents are inherited from zeta poles, so spectral information in the crossing equation is read through the residue structure of the shifted Eisenstein integral.

units.title: Scalar modular bootstrap and zeros of the Riemann zeta function

It then chooses an even rapidly decaying function phi with phi(0)=phi-hat(0)=0, forms Phi(t)=sum phi(nt), and defines the functional F_phi[h]=integral h(t)Phi(t)dt/t precisely to annihilate those zero-dependent power terms.

The strategy is projection rather than direct estimation. Instead of trying to control the sign-indefinite zeta-zero terms numerically, the paper engineers a functional whose Mellin behavior removes them from the sum rule altogether.

The inverse Laplace transform then turns that question into one about the integrated scalar density N_0(Delta) for small Delta.

The obstruction is the spectral gap below the first excited scalar. Requiring N_0(Delta) to vanish there forces one pole that fixes E_0^c(mu)=-1, rules out any other poles with Re(s)<1/2 except at zeros of the prefactor, and finally translates the allowed pole set back to the original integrand through the functional equation.

units.title: A new integral representation for the Riemann Zeta function

If F has a pole at s=1-delta_1, then the theorem says that F must have infinitely many poles in every right half-plane Re(s)>C, and for every Y>100 one such pole occurs within d log log Y of height Y.

The result is a rigidity statement about singularities. Good-Dirichlet-series structure does not allow one translated zeta pole to remain isolated; once one pole appears, the quotient is forced into persistent pole proliferation with explicit vertical localization.

The span distinguishes local witnesses from global certification. Counting sign changes of the completed zeta function on the critical line only produces on-line zeros one by one; by itself that does not exclude missed or off-line zeros.

The extra move is Turing-style completeness. units.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
units.selection_reason: Riemann moves from zero counting evidence to the conjecture, explicitly marks the missing proof, and then uses the zero representation without treating the conjecture as necessary for his next objective.
units.interpretation:
Riemann first uses an argument-principle count to estimate how many roots of xi lie in a bounded region, then reports that one indeed finds about that many real roots and says it is very probable that all roots are real. He immediately marks that stronger claim as unproved and unnecessary for his next step.

The operative move is disciplined separation of evidence and dependence. The source continues with a logarithmic product expansion over all roots alpha because that representation only needs control of root density and existence, not a proof that every root is real or an ordering of them on the line.

units.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
units.selection_reason: The Euler product is converted into a weighted prime-counting object and inverted through Mellin/Fourier machinery, exposing the bridge from primes to analytic singularities.
units.interpretation:
Riemann defines a symmetrized prime-counting function F and then folds prime powers into a weighted function f(x)=F(x)+1/2F(x^(1/2))+1/3F(x^(1/3))+.... With that choice, log zeta(s)/s becomes the Mellin transform of f for Re(s)>1.

The second step is inversion. By invoking Fourier's theorem in the Mellin setting, the paper writes f(y) back as a vertical-line integral of log zeta(s)/s times y^s. The unit is therefore a two-way transform bridge between weighted prime-counting data and analytic information in zeta, and it explicitly notes that naive termwise substitution does not yet converge, motivating the later integration-by-parts repair.

units.title: The De Bruijn-Newman constant is non-negative
units.selection_reason: Backward heat flow embeds RH into a monotone family with threshold Lambda, separating RH's upper bound from Newman's complementary 'barely true' lower bound.
units.interpretation:
The source embeds the RH question into the one-parameter family H_t evolving under backward heat flow. Newman provides the threshold constant Lambda such that H_t has only real zeros exactly for t >= Lambda, so RH becomes the upper bound Lambda <= 0. The paper's result is the complementary lower bound Lambda >= 0, obtained by contradiction.

The conceptual gain is that zero location becomes a dynamical boundary problem. Assuming Lambda < 0 forces increasingly rigid local-equilibrium behavior for zeros of H_0, and the source says that this rigidity conflicts with known local zero statistics for zeta, such as Montgomery-type pair-correlation information.

The overview starts from the counterfactual hypothesis Lambda<0 and says the paper no longer pursues only improved Lehmer-pair bounds. Instead it strengthens the repulsion picture to a local-relaxation-to-equilibrium picture: if Lambda were negative, the zeros of H_t would tend to arrange themselves locally like an approximate arithmetic progression with gaps close to the average spacing predicted by Riemann-von Mangoldt counts.

The proof strategy makes that claim quantitative by combining interval zero-counting formulas for H_t, the ODE evolution of zeros under backward heat flow, and Hamiltonian and energy functionals with monotonicity properties. After truncation and averaging, those controls force near-equilibrium behavior at t=0, and the source says that this prediction is then contradicted by known local zero statistics such as Montgomery pair correlation. The obstruction comes from the mismatch between forced equilibrium spacing and the actual local distribution.
